what_its_for: Cyclosporine is used to prevent your body from rejecting a transplanted organ (such as a kidney, liver, or heart). It works by calming down your immune system so it does not attack the new organ. It is also used to treat severe rheumatoid arthritis, a serious skin condition called psoriasis, and dry eye disease (eye drop form).
how_to_take: Take cyclosporine by mouth exactly as your doctor tells you. You can take it with or without food, but try to take it the same way every time — either always with food or always without food. Do not switch between different brands of cyclosporine without talking to your doctor first, because they are not interchangeable. If using the liquid form, use the special measuring syringe provided, mix the liquid in a glass of orange juice or apple juice (not grapefruit juice), stir well, and drink it right away. Rinse the glass with a little more juice and drink that too so you get the full dose. For eye drops (Restasis or Cequa), wash your hands before use, tilt your head back, pull down your lower eyelid, and place one drop into the affected eye. Remove contact lenses before putting in the drops and wait at least 15 minutes before putting them back in.
dosing: Your dose will be carefully calculated by your doctor based on your body weight, the condition being treated, and your kidney function. Doses are different for everyone. Most people take it twice a day, about 12 hours apart, at the same times each day. Do not change your dose on your own. Your doctor will do regular blood tests to make sure the level of cyclosporine in your blood is correct — not too high (which can cause side effects) and not too low (which may not work well enough).
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember — but only if it is not too close to the time for your next dose. If it is almost time for your next dose, skip the missed dose and continue on your regular schedule. Do not take two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one. If you are unsure what to do, call your doctor or pharmacist.
storage: Store cyclosporine capsules and liquid at room temperature, between 68°F and 77°F (20°C and 25°C). Keep away from heat, moisture, and direct light. Do not store in the bathroom. The liquid form should be used within 2 months of opening the bottle. Do not refrigerate the liquid — it may become thick and hard to measure. Keep all forms of this medicine out of reach of children. For eye drops, store at room temperature and discard any unused portion after opening, as directed on the package.
what_to_avoid: Avoid grapefruit and grapefruit juice completely while taking cyclosporine — they can raise the level of the drug in your blood to a dangerous level. Avoid prolonged sun exposure and tanning beds, as cyclosporine increases your risk of skin cancer; use sunscreen and protective clothing when outdoors. Avoid live vaccines (such as MMR or varicella) without checking with your doctor first. Avoid contact with people who are sick or have infections, since your immune system will be weaker. Do not take St. John's Wort, as it can lower the level of cyclosporine in your blood. Check with your doctor or pharmacist before taking any new medications, vitamins, or herbal supplements, as many drugs interact with cyclosporine.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away if you notice any of the following: signs of infection such as fever, chills, sore throat, or unusual tiredness; decreased urination or swelling in your legs or ankles (possible kidney problems); high blood pressure, severe headache, or vision changes; yellowing of the skin or eyes, dark urine, or upper right stomach pain (possible liver problems); unusual bruising or bleeding; muscle weakness or pain; seizures; or any signs of skin changes such as new growths or sores that do not heal. Also contact your doctor if you experience trembling or shaking of the hands, increased hair growth, or gum swelling, as these are common but manageable side effects.
when_it_works: For organ transplant prevention, cyclosporine begins working quickly — often within the first few days — and must be taken every day for as long as your doctor prescribes, which is usually lifelong for transplant patients. For rheumatoid arthritis or psoriasis, you may start to notice improvement within 4 to 8 weeks, but it can take up to 3 months to see the full benefit. For dry eye disease (eye drops), it may take 3 to 6 months of regular use before you notice a significant improvement in your symptoms. Do not stop taking cyclosporine without first talking to your doctor, even if you feel well.
special_populations: Older adults (65 and older): Use with caution. Older patients may be more sensitive to side effects such as kidney problems and high blood pressure. Close monitoring is needed. Pregnancy: Cyclosporine should only be used during pregnancy if clearly necessary and your doctor decides the benefits outweigh the risks. Talk to your doctor right away if you become pregnant or plan to become pregnant. Breastfeeding: Cyclosporine passes into breast milk and could harm a nursing baby. Talk to your doctor before breastfeeding. Children: Cyclosporine is used in children for certain conditions, but dosing is carefully adjusted by weight. Children should be closely monitored by their doctor. Kidney or liver disease: Your doctor may need to adjust your dose and will monitor your organ function more frequently.
